opus_only: Table 1 note describes EIV as the AR(2) fitted values and UIV as residuals (in-sample wording), unlike eq. (4) which is a one-step-ahead forecast.
UIV enters contemporaneously with the month's return; the note also lists one-month lagged EIV and ret-1, but no such rows have values in Table 2.
The size effect may be partly explained by idiosyncratic volatility, consistent with Fu (2009); left to future work.
Annual liquidity measures miss monthly variation and cannot give monthly liquidity shocks.
Table 4 monthly TAQ spreads (1993-2003): EIV and UIV stay significant with lagged spread and spread-change controls.
The five UIV portfolios hold different UIVs but similar EIV spread; measured by excess return and CAPM, FF3 and FF3+MOM alphas; rebalanced monthly.
High-minus-low leverage UIV slope difference is significant.
Because idiosyncratic volatility trended up from 1962 to 1997 (Campbell et al. 2001), the leverage test is repeated in two sub-periods.
Johnson (2004): with a constant asset premium, higher volatility lowers equity beta and expected equity return.
Leverage quintiles use the previous month's leverage ranking.
Conclusion claims monotone return/alpha increase from low to high UIV for both portfolio types (only value-weighted reported).
UIV's importance comes from the option effect (leverage-monotone slopes).
Expected returns are unobservable and no model estimates them well, so realized returns (ER + UR) are used as the dependent variable.
Fix: add a right-hand-side variable X correlated with UR (eq. A3).
sonnet_only: Standard theory says idiosyncratic risk earns no premium, which is the benchmark the paper tests against.
Aggregate-level studies of average idiosyncratic volatility versus market return also give mixed results.
The joint EIV/UIV result survives characteristic and liquidity controls and exchange exclusions.
Authors infer UIV's coefficient reflects unexpected returns, so EIV's coefficient, conditional on UIV, reflects expected return.
The paper differs from Fu and Spiegel-Wang by using daily-return IV with AR(2) decomposition rather than monthly EGARCH, while reaching a similar positive sign.
No agreed model for single-stock idiosyncratic volatility; EGARCH on monthly data used by Fu/Spiegel-Wang.
The monotonic leverage pattern of the UIV effect holds in every subperiod examined.
Factor data and risk-free rate come from Kenneth French's data library.
The contemporaneous positive UIV-return link does not by itself imply lower future returns.
IV for stock i in month m is the sum of squared daily residuals, following Ang et al. and Zhang.
EIV for month m+1 uses AR coefficients estimated through m applied to IV at m and m-1.
Alternative AR lag specifications give qualitatively the same main results.
Both components are needed: using total or expected volatility alone misses the EIV premium.
Two follow-up tests: UIV-sorted portfolios and leverage test of the option effect.
Conclusion repeats that Ang et al.'s negative realized return result addresses a different relation.
Leverage-monotonic UIV coefficients are taken as support that UIV matters through the option effect.
If a variable X is correlated with unexpected return, adding it (A3) absorbs the noise and corrects bias in the EIV coefficient.
Final claim: decomposing idiosyncratic volatility reveals both components significantly related to returns in different ways.
